title: I'm testing how far a team of AI agents can take a real game. Curious what you think
author: Elegant-Breakfast174
selftext:
Hi everyone,
    
    I'm a solo dev, and I'm running an experiment: building a small 3D roguelike with a team of Claude agents managed through Paperclip. There's a designer, an engineer, a reviewer, a producer and a marketing team, and they work through tasks while I act as the person who sets direction, plays the builds and approves things. The game is just the test case. What I really want to find out is whether this setup can get a game all the way to Steam.
    
    So far it works better than I expected for the boring but important parts: specs, code, reviews, planning. It works less well for anything that needs taste. No agent can tell me whether a dodge roll feels good, so that part stays with me. The agents also can't publish anything themselves. They prepare drafts and hand them to me, and I'm the one who posts.
    
    I'm well aware of the token cost. I'm on a Claude Pro plan, so when I run out I have to wait for the limit to reset, and that often sets the pace more than anything else. I don't know yet if the overhead of coordinating several agents pays off compared to just using one assistant.
    
    Do you think this is a sensible way to make a game, or is the overhead not worth it? And if you've tried something similar, what worked for you and what didn't?
    
    P.S. This post was written by the Marketing Lead agent of my team. I read it and posted it myself.

comments.author: gardens_and_dungeons
comments.body:
I'm building a custom-engine MMORPG using Codex and Claude, alongside a separate civilization simulation project, so I've experimented quite a bit with coordinating multiple agents.

My workflow developed organically rather than starting with an orchestration framework. The agents communicate through shared Markdown files, coordinate resource usage, review each other's work, and have built tools to help one another. I generally run separate sessions for different tasks and let them work for extended periods, using compaction rather than constantly restarting conversations.

What I've found is that the biggest challenge isn't necessarily the models or token usage. It's keeping the project organized, identifying recurring problems, and developing systems that prevent those problems from happening again.

I also wouldn't underestimate what a single agent can accomplish. Adding more agents doesn't automatically increase productivity, particularly when coordination consumes resources that could otherwise go toward development.

And I agree about human judgment. Automated tests can tell you whether a dodge roll works technically, but someone still needs to decide whether it actually feels good to play.

My advice would be to let the workflow evolve around problems you actually encounter rather than building a complicated management system in advance. Give the agents room to investigate and improve their tools, but verify their results.

I've been developing this way since starting with code generated in ChatGPT's free tier, and the process has changed considerably as I've learned what works.

Ultimately, I'd judge the setup by how much useful, verified progress it produces, not by how many agents are involved.

comments.author: Charming_You_25
comments.body:
What I think is that you are falling for the 2 week demo high.

\- Game design is no where near solved.   
\- Game design is an iterative process.   
\- Handing agents judgement of “is this good” produces extremely boring results. You may be doing this more than you think.  
\- Adding features over refining design is a trap that AI makes extremely easy to fall into.  
\- it takes 1-2 weeks for a demo that makes you feel almost done. 6 months to something you’re embarrassed about. And years before it’s good. Even with AI.

replies.author: ai_helps
replies.body: The adding features part is true.  I see it in my own business application development all the time.  I used to do it anyway.  Now it's on steroids.

comments.author: toroidalvoid
comments.body:
Getting something on Steam is probably the wrong goal/framing, otherwise what you're describing is a slop factory.

What you want to build is a game so fun that sharing on steam is a right channel for it, should you want to to publish it.

I dont know what paperclip is or where the idea that you should have long running sessions. Agents work best when they have a clear goal in the first promt and can finish within ~20% context.

But its a good thing to try, its the latest version of trying to get agents to run for longer unattended and get good results and is applicable to any project. Unfortunately I dont have good enough results woth sharing yet - still early days
